title: Circles: circumference and area
blurb: Use radius and diameter correctly, find circumference and area with 3.14 for pi, and work backward or around composite circular shapes.
question: A circular flower bed has a radius of 5 ft and is surrounded by a path 2 ft wide. Using 3.14 for pi, what is the area of the path alone?

teach.body: Formally, a circle is the set of points a fixed distance (the radius, r) from a center point. The diameter (d) runs edge to edge through the center, so d = 2r. Pi (π) is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14. In plain English: go around any circle and you travel a little over 3 diameters. TEAS circle questions tell you to use 3.14 for π, so use exactly 3.14.

teach.h: The four facts behind every circle question

items.label: the value to use on the TEAS

teach.caption: r² means r × r. Square the radius first, then multiply by 3.14.

teach.h: Worked example: a circular garden, diameter 10 m
items: Circumference: C = πd = 3.14 × 10 = 31.4 m of edging. Check with 2πr: 2 × 3.14 × 5 = 31.4 m.
Area: first halve the diameter, r = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 m. Then r² = 5 × 5 = 25.

teach.h: Read the givens before you pick a formula
teach.caption: The most common error is using the diameter in A = πr².

teach.body: From a circumference, divide by 3.14 to get the diameter, then halve for the radius: C = 47.1 in gives d = 47.1 ÷ 3.14 = 15 in and r = 7.5 in. From an area, divide by 3.14 to get r², then take the square root: A = 113.04 ft² gives r² = 113.04 ÷ 3.14 = 36, so r = 6 ft and d = 12 ft. Stopping at r² is a classic slip.

teach.h: Area grows with the square of the radius
teach.caption: Double the radius (1 to 2, or 2 to 4) and the area becomes 4 times as big, while the circumference only doubles.

teach.body: Aaliyah, a physical-therapy aide applying to nursing school, needs to know how far a wheelchair rolls in 50 turns of a wheel 24 in across. One turn covers the circumference: C = 3.14 × 24 = 75.36 in. Fifty turns: 75.36 × 50 = 3,768 in. In feet: 3,768 ÷ 12 = 314 ft. A semicircle works the same way: its perimeter is half the circumference plus the straight diameter, πd ÷ 2 + d.

teach.text: Radius or diameter? A = πr² needs the radius: with a diameter of 8, use r = 4 (area 50.24), not 8 (area 200.96). Also watch for circumference given when area was asked, and stopping at r² when working backward from an area.

items: Area A = πr² (square units): halve the diameter first.
Backward: d = C ÷ 3.14; r² = A ÷ 3.14, then square root.
Composite shapes: semicircle perimeter = πd ÷ 2 + d; rings and cut-outs = bigger area minus smaller area.

summary: You can now move between radius and diameter, find circumference and area with 3.14 for π, and work backward from either one. You can also handle semicircles, rings, wheels and shapes with circles cut out of them.

A.q: A circular rug has a diameter of 8 ft. Using 3.14 for π, what is its area?

whyNot.0: This uses the diameter as the radius: 3.14 × 8 × 8.
whyNot.1: This is the circumference (3.14 × 8), not the area.
whyNot.3: This doubles the area, mixing the 2 from 2πr into the area formula.

A.q: A circular table has a radius of 18 in. Using 3.14 for π, what is its circumference?

whyNot.1: This multiplies π by the radius only (3.14 × 18); it needs the diameter.
whyNot.2: This is the area (3.14 × 18²), not the circumference.

A.q: A small pizza has a diameter of 10 in and a large pizza has a diameter of 20 in. Using 3.14 for π, how much more area does the large pizza have?

whyNot.0: This is the difference in circumference (62.8 - 31.4), not area.
whyNot.1: This uses the diameters as radii (1,256 - 314).
whyNot.2: 314 is the large pizza's whole area, not how much more it has.

B.q: A circular running track has a circumference of 942 m. Using 3.14 for π, what is its radius, to the nearest tenth?

whyNot.0: 300 m is the diameter; the radius is half of it.
whyNot.2: This treats 942 as an area and takes the square root of 942 ÷ 3.14.
whyNot.3: This halves the circumference (942 ÷ 2) but never divides by 3.14.

B.q: A round tabletop has an area of 28.26 ft². Using 3.14 for π, what is its diameter?

whyNot.0: 3 ft is the radius; the question asks for the diameter.
whyNot.1: This stops at r² = 9 without taking the square root.
whyNot.2: This divides by 2π (6.28), treating the area as a circumference.

B.q: A semicircular window has a diameter of 4 ft. Using 3.14 for π, what is the perimeter of the window, including the straight bottom edge?
B.why: Curved edge: half of πd = 3.14 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6.28 ft. Add the straight diameter: 6.28 + 4 = 10.28 ft.

whyNot.0: This is the curved edge only; the straight bottom edge is missing.
whyNot.1: This is the full circle's circumference, not half.
whyNot.3: This uses the full circumference and then adds the diameter.

C.q: A circular flower bed has a radius of 5 ft and is surrounded by a path 2 ft wide. Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of the path alone?
C.why: Outer radius = 5 + 2 = 7 ft. Outer area 3.14 × 49 = 153.86 ft². Bed 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 ft². Path: 153.86 - 78.5 = 75.36 ft².

whyNot.1: This is the whole outer circle, including the flower bed.
whyNot.2: This adds the 2 ft to the diameter instead of the radius (outer r = 6 ft).
whyNot.3: This finds the area of a circle with radius 2 ft, the path width.

C.q: A bicycle wheel has a diameter of 26 in. Using 3.14 for π, how many complete revolutions does the wheel make in 1,000 ft?
C.why: Same units: 1,000 ft × 12 = 12,000 in. One revolution = 3.14 × 26 = 81.64 in. 12,000 ÷ 81.64 = 146.98, so 146 complete revolutions.

whyNot.0: This rounds 146.98 up; the 147th revolution is not complete.
whyNot.2: This uses the radius in C = πd (3.14 × 13).
whyNot.3: This uses 2 × π × the diameter, twice the real circumference.

C.q: A square tile 10 in on each side has the largest possible circle painted inside it. Using 3.14 for π, what area of the tile is NOT painted?
C.why: The circle's diameter is 10 in, so r = 5 in and A = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 in². Tile: 10 × 10 = 100 in². Unpainted: 100 - 78.5 = 21.5 in².

whyNot.0: 78.5 in² is the painted circle, not the part left over.
whyNot.1: This subtracts the circumference (31.4) from the square's area.
whyNot.2: This is the circle's circumference, not an area.

reteach.title: Think of a bike wheel and a pizza
reteach.question: A bike wheel rolling along and a pizza on a table are both circles. Which one is about circumference and which is about area?

blocks.body: When a wheel turns once, the tire's edge touches the road all the way around: one turn moves the bike one circumference. That is a length. A pizza is about how much there is to eat: the cheese covers the whole surface, which is area. Wheels and fences are circumference questions; pizzas, rugs and lawns are area questions. And a pizza described as "12 inch" is giving the diameter, so its radius is 6.

blocks.text: Sizes of round things (pizzas, pans, tables) are usually given as the diameter. Halve it before using A = πr².

explain.body: The radius goes from the center to the edge; the diameter goes all the way across through the center. d = 2r, so r = d ÷ 2.

test.q: A circular clock face has a diameter of 30 cm. What is the distance from the center to the edge?
test.why: Center to edge is the radius: r = 30 ÷ 2 = 15 cm.

whyNot.0: This doubles the diameter instead of halving it.
whyNot.2: This halves twice; 7.5 cm is a quarter of the diameter.
whyNot.3: This is the circumference (3.14 × 30), the distance around.

explain.body: C = πd, or C = 2πr. With a diameter of 9 m: C = 3.14 × 9 = 28.26 m.

test.q: Using 3.14 for π, what is the circumference of a circle with a diameter of 9 m?

whyNot.1: This uses 2πr with the diameter in place of r, doubling the answer.
whyNot.2: This is the area (3.14 × 4.5²), not the circumference.
whyNot.3: This multiplies π by the radius only.

explain.body: A = πr². Square the radius, then multiply by 3.14. With r = 1.5 yd: 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25, and 3.14 × 2.25 = 7.065 yd².

test.q: Using 3.14 for π, what is the area of a circle with a radius of 1.5 yd, to the nearest hundredth?

whyNot.1: This uses the diameter (3 yd) as the radius: 3.14 × 9.
whyNot.2: This multiplies π by r instead of r².

explain.body: Circumference to area: d = C ÷ 3.14, r = d ÷ 2, then A = 3.14 × r². C = 31.4 cm gives d = 10, r = 5, A = 78.5 cm².

test.q: Using 3.14 for π, a circle has a circumference of 31.4 cm. What is its area?

whyNot.0: This uses the diameter, 10 cm, as the radius.
